title: Villager
summary: A figure in two facings, feet on a tile, with shadow and outline layers.

tips.title: Feet on the tile.
tips.text: The feet sit on the center of a tile, so the figure stands in the right place wherever it goes on a map.

tips.title: Shade along a ramp.
tips.text: Every color here is a step on a palette ramp: lighter toward the light on the left, darker away from it. No black or white is mixed in. Lighten / Darken moves a pixel one step.

tips.title: Sel-out.
tips.text: The outline is one ramp step darker than the pixels beside it, not black. It separates the figure from the ground without a hard line, and it sits on its own layer.

tips.title: One light, one shadow.
tips.text: The shadow falls away from the light and stays on its own layer at 35 percent, so you can change it without touching the figure.

tips.title: Two facings are enough.
tips.text: Draw one facing toward you and one facing away. Mirror each and you have all four.

lesson: Feet on a tile, two facings, and shadow and outline on their own layers.
author: claude

title: Cottage yard
summary: A house, a well and a tree built from objects. Explode the house to edit its pieces.

tips.title: One tap, the whole house.
tips.text: The house is an assembly. Select object picks all of it, so it moves and turns as one. Explode takes it apart into pieces you can edit.

tips.title: Change one part.
tips.text: Double-tap the house, or use Edit inside, to change one piece and keep the group together. Done or Esc leaves.

tips.title: 2:1 edges.
tips.text: Every slanted edge steps two pixels across for one down, never 30 or 45 degrees. Roof, walls and ground all use the same stair, so they meet cleanly.

tips.title: One light direction.
tips.text: This project is lit from the right, so walls facing right are lighter and shadows fall left. Choose Left: every face and shadow redraws, because objects keep their parameters.

tips.title: Big shapes first.
tips.text: The house began as a box and a roof. The door, windows and chimney came last. Blocks read at a glance, and details are easy to move once the blocks are right.

lesson: Build with objects, and they stay editable as one assembly.
author: claude

title: Village corner
summary: Terrain, a path, a fenced house, trees, water and a character, on separate layers.

tips.title: A layer for each job.
tips.text: Background, ground, terrain, props and the character each have their own layer, so you can hide, lock or repaint one without touching the others.

tips.title: Test tiles 3 x 3.
tips.text: The ground is stamped tiles in several variants. The preview repeats one tile 3 x 3, where any seam would show at once.

tips.title: Two levels of terrain.
tips.text: The hill comes from the Terrain tool. Each cell is a stack of levels, kept as ordinary objects you can still edit.

tips.title: Scatter, then reroll.
tips.text: The trees and rocks were painted with Scatter. The same stroke and seed give the same result, and Reroll tries another layout.

tips.title: Shadows that follow.
tips.text: Objects cast live shadows into a linked layer. Move anything and its shadow moves too, away from the one light in the project.

tips.title: On the ground.
tips.text: The character is plain pixels on a layer above the props, with feet on a tile center and a short shadow of its own.

lesson: A scene from tiles, terrain, scattered objects and live shadows.
author: claude

title: Crate
lesson: Three faces, one light: top, lit side, shaded side.
summary: Three faces, one light: top, lit side, shaded side.
author: claude

tips.title: Look at the whole crate.
tips.text: Three faces and one light from the left. The stages below take it apart, so tap 1 to 5 and then Finished.

tips.title: Block in the shape.
tips.text: One flat color for the silhouette. If this does not read as a box, no shading will save it.

tips.title: Step along the ramp.
tips.text: The top is the lightest, the lit side a step down and the shaded side darkest. Every color is a step on one ramp, with no black or white mixed in.

tips.title: Add the details last.
tips.text: Plank gaps and the braces follow the faces, so a brace on the left side leans the other way from one on the right.

tips.title: Outline with the art's own ramp.
tips.text: Sel-out: each outline pixel is a step darker than the pixel beside it, so the crate sits on any background. Try it yourself with the Outline button.

title: Barrel
lesson: Ellipse rims at 2:1, and banded shading on a round side.
summary: Ellipse rims at 2:1, and banded shading on a round side.
author: claude

tips.title: Look at the barrel.
tips.text: A round thing still follows the grid: its rim is an ellipse twice as wide as it is tall, the same 2:1 as a tile.

tips.title: Shade in bands.
tips.text: A curved side has no single face, so the light falls in vertical bands. Lightest a third of the way in from the left, a step per band, darkest on the right.

tips.title: Hoops curve with the rim.
tips.text: A straight hoop would flatten the barrel. These dip in the middle, like the front of the rim, so the form stays round.

tips.title: Try it.
tips.text: Run Lighten / Darken down one band and see how little it takes to make the barrel shinier or duller.

title: Bush
lesson: Clustered 3:2 shapes and a dithered edge.
summary: Clustered 3:2 shapes and a dithered edge.
author: claude

tips.title: Look at the bush.
tips.text: Foliage is not one blob. It is a few 3:2 ovals overlapping, each lit on its own upper left.

tips.title: Light each cluster.
tips.text: Every oval gets its own step of light, with the deepest dark where they meet at the bottom. Forms read from their shadows.

tips.title: Break the edge, then add berries.
tips.text: Pixels knocked out of the rim make it leafy rather than smooth, and a checker of two greens does the same inside. A few red pixels last.

tips.title: Try it.
tips.text: Dither with a checker over the right side and watch it turn from flat green into leaves.

title: Grass tile
lesson: A 2:1 diamond, and how it repeats 3 x 3 with no seam.
summary: A 2:1 diamond, and how it repeats 3 x 3 with no seam.
author: claude

tips.title: Look at one tile.
tips.text: This diamond is 24 pixels wide and 12 tall: always 2 across for 1 down. Everything on the path stands on this shape. Tap the stages, then Finished.

tips.title: Draw the diamond first.
tips.text: The edges climb in runs of 2 pixels, never smoother. That stair is what lets tiles lock together. One flat color is enough to check it.

tips.title: Keep texture off the border.
tips.text: The tufts stay a pixel or two inside the edge, so the seam between two tiles has nothing to line up.

tips.title: Now repeat it.
tips.text: The preview lays this tile out 3 x 3. Look for a line or a shape that gives the tile away. The outline is left out there, because tiles in a floor touch.

title: Stone path and water
lesson: Two tiles that join, and ramp offsets for texture.
summary: Two tiles that join, and ramp offsets for texture.
author: claude

tips.title: Look at the two tiles.
tips.text: Stone on the left, water on the right, sharing one edge. Each repeats by itself, and the edge between them is a straight 2:1 stair, so either can sit beside the other.

tips.title: One color, then offsets.
tips.text: The cobbles are one mid step with gaps one or two steps darker, and a corner a step lighter. Texture comes from moving along the ramp, not from new colors.

tips.title: Water is mostly one color.
tips.text: A few short dashes a step lighter and darker run along the grid. They imply ripples, and leaving most of the tile flat keeps it calm.

tips.title: Now repeat the stone.
tips.text: Three by three, the cobbles carry on across the seams, as the pattern repeats exactly once per tile.

title: Mailbox and bench
lesson: Small props, and sel-out outlines.
summary: Small props, and sel-out outlines.
author: claude

tips.title: Look at the two props.
tips.text: A bench and a mailbox, each just a handful of parts. Small things read through a clear silhouette, not through detail.

tips.title: Parts first.
tips.text: Planks, legs, box and post get one color each. If two parts merge here, the outline will not separate them later.

tips.title: One red flag.
tips.text: One small accent does a lot: the flag says mailbox more than the box does. Keep accents few, and in a color the piece does not otherwise use.

tips.title: Sel-out keeps it soft.
tips.text: Each outline pixel is one step darker than the art beside it, so the wood gets a brown line and the box a blue one. A black line would look stuck on.

tips.title: Try it.
tips.text: Pick the bench planks with the Color picker and step one with Lighten / Darken to see a plank stand out.

title: Pine
lesson: Stacked flattened cones, each hem an ellipse.
summary: Stacked flattened cones, each hem an ellipse.
author: claude

tips.title: Look at the pine.
tips.text: Four cones stacked, each smaller than the one below. The bottom of every cone is a piece of a 2:1 ellipse, so the tree stands on the same grid as a tile.

tips.title: One silhouette.
tips.text: Lay out the four tiers as a jagged arrow. Getting the steps even matters more than any detail.

tips.title: Bands, like the barrel.
tips.text: A cone is round, so each tier gets vertical bands: lit on the left, dark on the right. The same idea as the barrel, on a slant.

tips.title: Pick out the hems.
tips.text: Light pixels along the left of each hem separate one tier from the next, and scallops stop the edge looking cut with a ruler.

title: Rock
lesson: Value planes on an irregular form.
summary: Value planes on an irregular form.
author: claude

tips.title: Look at the rock.
tips.text: No face of it lines up with the grid, but it is still a top, a lit side and a shaded side.

tips.title: Think in flat planes.
tips.text: Four values, each a flat shape with straight edges. Curves make a rock look soft; corners make it hard.

tips.title: Try it.
tips.text: Cracks go where two planes meet. Add a dark line along one edge with the Pencil and the rock gets harder.

title: Street lamp
lesson: Thin vertical forms, and a glow made with dither.
summary: Thin vertical forms, and a glow made with dither.
author: claude

tips.title: Look at the lamp.
tips.text: A post two pixels wide is hard to shade, so it gets one light column and one dark one. That is all a thin form needs.

tips.title: Parts, one color each.
tips.text: Base, post, collar, lantern, cap. At this stage it should already read as a street lamp, with nothing but its silhouette.

tips.title: Glow is a pattern, not a blend.
tips.text: Pixels here are opaque, so light cannot fade. A checker near the lantern, then sparser dots, and the eye mixes them with the dusk behind.

tips.title: Try it.
tips.text: Put a dark layer behind the lamp and the glow comes up. Dither is the tool that made it.

title: Tree
lesson: A tapered trunk, foliage ovals and a ground shadow.
summary: A tapered trunk, foliage ovals and a ground shadow.
author: claude

tips.title: Look at the tree.
tips.text: A trunk, a crown of ovals, and a shadow on the ground. It stands on a tile: the base of the trunk is on the center of a cell.

tips.title: Big shapes first.
tips.text: The whole silhouette in one color. A tree reads from its outline: wide crown, narrow trunk, a bit of flare at the ground.

tips.title: Each oval has its own light.
tips.text: Top left of every cluster is light, and the bottom right falls into the next one. The lowest row is the darkest, as the crown shades itself.

tips.title: Bark comes last.
tips.text: The trunk is three vertical bands, wider at the base. A few dark marks are enough.

tips.title: The shadow is its own layer.
tips.text: It falls away from the light and stays at 35 percent, so it can change without touching the tree. It came from Cast shadow.

title: Campfire
lesson: A warm ramp, and a lit area on the ground.
summary: A warm ramp, and a lit area on the ground.
author: claude

tips.title: Look at the fire.
tips.text: The stones sit in a 2:1 ellipse and the logs run along the grid. Only the flame ignores the grid, because it is the one thing here that moves.

tips.title: A flame is one ramp.
tips.text: Red-orange outside, yellow inside, almost white at the heart. Each tongue is the same shape, a step lighter and a size smaller.

tips.title: Try it.
tips.text: The light on the ground is a checker, then sparser dots, with nothing blended. Dither a wider ring and the fire looks brighter.

title: Cat (sitting)
lesson: Ears, a tail, and the same body plan as the dog.
summary: Ears, a tail, and the same body plan as the dog.
author: claude

tips.title: Compare it with the dog.
tips.text: Same plan: head up, chest, haunch, tail. Pointed ears, a short face and an upright tail do the rest.

tips.title: Change the ends.
tips.text: Most of an animal is one body. Swap the head and tail and a dog turns into a cat, so start from those.

tips.title: Same ramp plan.
tips.text: Light on the head and chest, dark on the low back, like the dog on a redder ramp. Pale eyes stand out against it, so they are the one detail it needs.

tips.title: The other facing.
tips.text: The tail is what a mirror shows up: it swaps sides with the head, so the whole cat looks the other way. Nothing needed redrawing.

title: Child
lesson: Proportions at 3 heads tall.
summary: Proportions at 3 heads tall.
author: claude

tips.title: Compare the head.
tips.text: Seven rows of head on twenty-one rows of child: three heads tall. The Walker has a head nearly this big on a much longer body. Proportions say child, not size.

tips.title: Measure in heads.
tips.text: Block the head, then stack two more of the same height, one for the body and one for the legs. Big head, no neck.

tips.title: Few details.
tips.text: Two eyes low on the face and one pixel of blush. Moving the eyes down makes a face younger.

tips.title: Try it.
tips.text: Scale nothing. Erase two rows of leg and see how much younger it gets.

title: Courier with a parcel
lesson: Carried objects, and what goes wrong in a mirror.
summary: Carried objects, and what goes wrong in a mirror.
author: claude

tips.title: Look at the courier.
tips.text: The parcel hides the middle of the figure, so it is drawn as part of the same pose: arms under it, weight leaning back a little.

tips.title: Pose with the load.
tips.text: Merge the figure and the parcel into one shape. If the two look stuck together rather than carried, move the arms, not the box.

tips.title: A box still has three faces.
tips.text: The parcel is the crate again, small: light top, mid left, dark right, and a label to say which way up it goes.

tips.title: Mirrors flip everything.
tips.text: The label and the cap peak swap sides, and the light does too. A flip is fine for most things, but look at text and at anything held in one hand.

title: Dog (sitting)
lesson: Animal silhouette, a fur ramp, facing and mirror.
summary: Animal silhouette, a fur ramp, facing and mirror.
author: claude

tips.title: Look at the dog.
tips.text: Sitting is the easiest pose to read: head up, chest forward, haunch low, tail on the ground.

tips.title: A silhouette, not an outline.
tips.text: Snout, back, tail. You should know it is a dog from this one flat shape.

tips.title: The ear goes on last.
tips.text: A floppy ear two steps darker sits inside the silhouette, so it has to wait for the details. That one patch says dog more than anything else.

tips.title: Fur is a ramp.
tips.text: The light chest and muzzle are one step on the same ramp as the darker back. No new color, just a shift along it.

tips.title: The other facing.
tips.text: Animals face a way, so a flip gives you the second one for nothing. Most animals are close enough to symmetric that nobody notices.

title: Duck
lesson: Rounded forms in a few pixels.
summary: Rounded forms in a few pixels.
author: claude

tips.title: Look at the duck.
tips.text: A curve for the back, a curve for the neck, a dot for an eye. At this size one misplaced pixel changes the animal.

tips.title: Two ovals.
tips.text: A low wide one and a small high one, joined by a neck. Any bird starts like this.

tips.title: Try it.
tips.text: The bill and feet are the only warm pixels. Move the eye one pixel with the Pencil and see how much the duck changes.

title: Gardener
lesson: Clothing ramps, and hat and tool silhouettes.
summary: Clothing ramps, and hat and tool silhouettes.
author: claude

tips.title: Look at the gardener.
tips.text: A wide hat and a long-handled spade say gardener before any detail does. Cover them with a thumb and it could be anyone.

tips.title: Silhouette first.
tips.text: Hat brim wider than the shoulders, tool taller than the head. Props that stick out of the shape read best.

tips.title: Each garment a ramp.
tips.text: Straw, shirt, overalls and skin each step along their own ramp, so clothes look like separate things and not one painted shape.

tips.title: Shade under the brim.
tips.text: One dark row across the top of the face puts the hat on the head. Without it the hat floats.

title: Rabbit
lesson: One ramp, and a strong silhouette.
summary: One ramp, and a strong silhouette.
author: claude

tips.title: Look at the rabbit.
tips.text: Every pixel is on one ramp. With a silhouette this clear, the long ears do all the work.

tips.title: Ears make it.
tips.text: Two tall lines on a round body, one step apart, so the sky shows between them.

tips.title: Try it.
tips.text: Erase the top of the ears and it turns into a mouse. One ramp keeps a sprite this small clean, so the shape has to do the work.

title: Walker
lesson: Feet on a tile, and two facings from one drawing.
summary: Feet on a tile, and two facings from one drawing.
author: claude

tips.title: Look at the two figures.
tips.text: The one on the right is not a second drawing. It is the left one flipped, on a linked layer.

tips.title: Pose in one color.
tips.text: A stride reads from the gap between the legs and the arm swung opposite. If the silhouette walks, the rest will.

tips.title: Ramps for clothes too.
tips.text: Jacket, trousers and skin each have a ramp, lit from the left. Three or four steps is plenty at this size.

tips.title: Feet on the tile.
tips.text: The pivot is on the center of a cell, between the feet, so the figure stands in the right place anywhere on a map. Set pivot shows it.

tips.title: Mirror, then update.
tips.text: Draw one facing only. Update mirror, in the Character section, redoes the flip after an edit. Remember that the light flips too.

title: Car
lesson: A box with a cabin, glass and wheel arches.
summary: A box with a cabin, glass and wheel arches.
author: claude

tips.title: Look at the car.
tips.text: Two boxes on the grid: a long low one and a shorter one on top. The long side faces the light.

tips.title: Two boxes.
tips.text: Block the body and the cabin first. The proportions decide whether it is a car, a van or a truck.

tips.title: Glass is a value, not a color.
tips.text: The windows are a light cool ramp on the lit side and darker in front, with a slanted streak. They follow the same light as the paint.

tips.title: Wheels sit in arches.
tips.text: A dark ring first and the wheel inside it, both skewed to lie on the side of the car. The wheels touch the tile, so the car stands on the grid.

title: Cow
lesson: Two-tone patches that follow the form.
summary: Two-tone patches that follow the form.
author: claude

tips.title: Look at the cow.
tips.text: A long body on four legs, turned along the grid, with a big square head. It faces the same way a car would.

tips.title: A box with a head.
tips.text: The body is a box on the grid, so it sits on tiles like a crate. Four short legs and a tail make it an animal.

tips.title: Patches wrap around.
tips.text: A dark patch runs over the back and on down the side, changing shape at the corner. Spots that ignore the corner look printed on.

tips.title: The nose says cow.
tips.text: The pink muzzle, a step or two along its own ramp, is the part nobody could mistake.

title: Van
lesson: Reusing the car's plan with different proportions.
summary: Reusing the car's plan with different proportions.
author: claude

tips.title: Compare it with the car.
tips.text: The same wheels, glass and lamps, but one tall box instead of two. Change the proportions and the plan still holds.

tips.title: One tall box.
tips.text: A van is a little shorter than you expect and much higher than the car. Nothing else about the block-in is new.

tips.title: White is not white.
tips.text: The lightest step is the top only. The lit side is a step down and the shaded side two, or the form disappears.

tips.title: A stripe wraps the corner.
tips.text: It runs down the side at one height and carries on across the front, a step darker there, which ties the two faces together.

title: Bicycle
lesson: Thin shapes, and wheels as 2:1 ellipses.
summary: Thin shapes, and wheels as 2:1 ellipses.
author: claude

tips.title: Look at the bicycle.
tips.text: Almost nothing but lines. Both wheels lie on the side of an invisible box that runs along the grid, so they lean the same way as a wall.

tips.title: Wheels first.
tips.text: Two skewed rings give the size and the direction. The frame goes between them, and its triangle is what says bicycle.

tips.title: Only the tires are outlined.
tips.text: An outline on a 1 pixel tube fills the gaps, so the frame goes on after the outline and stands alone.

tips.title: Spokes are a hint.
tips.text: A cross of dim pixels is enough. A full set would fill the wheel in and lose the silhouette.

title: Motorcycle
lesson: Mass and detail, wheels and a tank.
summary: Mass and detail, wheels and a tank.
author: claude

tips.title: Look at the motorcycle.
tips.text: The same two wheels as the bicycle, with something heavy between them. Where the bicycle was air, this is solid.

tips.title: Mass between the wheels.
tips.text: The block-in fills the frame. Tank, seat and engine are one lump that leans slightly forward.

tips.title: The tank catches the light.
tips.text: It is the only smooth rounded part, so it gets the widest ramp and a highlight along the top.

tips.title: Dark details on dark.
tips.text: The engine is two steps of gray with a row of fins. Near black needs only a little contrast to read.

title: Sailboat
lesson: Long forms on water, and a hull on the iso axis.
summary: Long forms on water, and a hull on the iso axis.
author: claude

tips.title: Look at the boat.
tips.text: A hull runs along the grid like a wall, but it comes to a point. Sails stand in the same plane as the hull, so they lean with it.

tips.title: Hull, mast, two triangles.
tips.text: A boat is a very short list of shapes. Most of the work is in where they meet.

tips.title: Sails are lit too.
tips.text: White cloth still has steps: lightest at the top where it faces the sky, a step down toward the boom.

tips.title: Water marks.
tips.text: A few dashes on the tile say water. Too many and the boat stops being the subject.

title: Small plane
lesson: An object turned to the iso axis, with wings as thin slabs.
summary: An object turned to the iso axis, with wings as thin slabs.
author: claude

tips.title: Look at the plane.
tips.text: A tube along one grid axis and a long thin slab along the other. Turn anything to the grid first, and the rest is boxes.

tips.title: The cross.
tips.text: Body and wing make a plus laid on the ground. The tail is a small copy of it.

tips.title: Wings are thin slabs.
tips.text: A wing is a top face and a thin edge, two pixels deep. The top catches all the light. Draw the far wing first and the near one last, with the body between.

tips.title: One stripe, end to end.
tips.text: A red line along the body and red wing tips tell the eye that the far parts belong to the same plane.

title: Train engine
lesson: Repeating parts along the axis.
summary: Repeating parts along the axis.
author: claude

tips.title: Look at the engine.
tips.text: Long things are mostly the same part again and again. Draw one wheel well and copy it along the axis.

tips.title: Three masses.
tips.text: Frame, boiler and cab. The boiler is a half cylinder pushed along the grid, the same trick as the mailbox.

tips.title: Bands along the tube.
tips.text: Along a cylinder the light runs in long stripes, as on the barrel but lying down. Brass rings break it into even lengths.

tips.title: Repeat, then break the rhythm.
tips.text: Three big wheels and two small ones, and one rod joining them. A pattern with an exception looks designed.

title: Street corner
lesson: Small examples placed on cell centers make a street.
summary: Small examples placed on cell centers make a street.
author: claude

tips.title: Look at the street.
tips.text: Every car, tree and person here is one of the small examples, standing on the center of a cell. Nothing was drawn for this scene but the ground.

tips.title: This car is the Car example.
tips.text: A scene is mostly placing. Each part is one layer, so you can move it or swap it for something you drew yourself.

tips.title: Shadows are live.
tips.text: Pixel art cannot cast a live shadow, so each part has a plain box on Shadow shapes, a layer at 0 opacity. Move a box with Select object and its shadow follows.

tips.title: Back to front.
tips.text: Layers go from the far corner to the near one, so what stands nearer covers what is behind it. The layer list reads like walking toward the viewer.

tips.title: Roads are tiles.
tips.text: Road, pavement and grass came from the Tile tool, each with its own texture. The pavement has a rim on its lower edges, which is the kerb.

title: Harbour
lesson: Water tiles, a quay and small props make a harbour.
summary: Water tiles, a quay and small props make a harbour.
author: claude

tips.title: Look at the harbour.
tips.text: Crates, barrels, the lamp and the walker are all examples from the path. Water is most of the picture and it is one tile, repeated.

tips.title: This boat is the Sailboat example.
tips.text: Its own patch of water is left out here, as the scene has water already. The hull sits on the tile just as it did alone.

tips.title: A cat on a crate.
tips.text: The cat stands on the same cell as the crate, drawn 9 pixels higher and on a layer above it. Height is just a shift up the screen.

tips.title: A quay is a tile with a rim.
tips.text: The stone tile has a rim on its lower edges, 8 pixels tall, which turns a flat floor into a wall above the water.

tips.title: Gulls are five pixels.
tips.text: Small sprites scattered over open water give the picture scale and life, for almost no work. Try a few more.

title: Apple
lesson: One ramp: base, shadow, highlight.
summary: One ramp: base, shadow, highlight.
author: claude

tips.title: Look at the apple.
tips.text: Almost every pixel of the fruit is one of four steps on the Brick ramp. No black and no white went in.

tips.title: Base, shadow, highlight.
tips.text: Base first. The shadow is one step down, on the side away from the light. The light side is one step up.

tips.title: Try it.
tips.text: Pick the Lighten / Darken tool and stroke along the bottom of the apple. Each pixel moves one step along its ramp, so the shading stays clean.

title: Cat face
lesson: Readable features with few pixels.
summary: Readable features with few pixels.
author: claude

tips.title: Look at the face.
tips.text: Two ears, two eyes and a nose. That is few pixels, and each one has a job, so nothing here is decoration.

tips.title: The shape says cat first.
tips.text: Before any feature, the wide head and two points already say cat. If this stage reads as a blob, a face will not save it.

tips.title: Try it.
tips.text: With the Pencil, move one black pupil a pixel to the side. Now the cat is looking at something. Features this small are all expression.

title: Heart
lesson: A clean silhouette and a 1 px outline.
summary: A clean silhouette and a 1 px outline.
author: claude

tips.title: Look at the heart.
tips.text: One color and one outline. It reads at any size because the shape does all the work.

tips.title: Start with the silhouette.
tips.text: Fill the shape in one color. Each edge steps one pixel at a time with no stray corners, and the two lobes match.

tips.title: Try the outline.
tips.text: With the Eraser, take one pixel out of the notch at the top. Then press Outline layer under Shadow and outline. The 1 px line follows the new shape.

title: House icon
lesson: Sel-out outlines and a limited palette.
summary: Sel-out outlines and a limited palette.
author: claude

tips.title: Look at the house.
tips.text: A handful of colors from DB16, and no black line anywhere. Everything is on three small ramps.

tips.title: Sel-out.
tips.text: The outline is not one color. Each outline pixel is a step darker than the art beside it: orange by the walls, deep blue by the roof. The house sits softly on any background.

tips.title: Try it.
tips.text: Tap the wall, the door and the chimney with the Color picker. They are all steps on one Oranges ramp. Reusing colors is what a limited palette means.

title: Leaf
lesson: Hue shift: shadows cooler, lights warmer.
summary: Hue shift: shadows cooler, lights warmer.
author: claude

tips.title: Look at the leaf.
tips.text: Dark green here is bluer than mid green, and light green is yellower. The color changes as well as the brightness.

tips.title: Follow one ramp.
tips.text: The Greens ramp is built that way: each step down moves toward blue and each step up toward yellow. Shading along it gives the hue shift for free.

tips.title: Try it.
tips.text: Tap a dark pixel with the Color picker, then a light one, and watch the hue slider move. Lit and shaded greens are different hues.

title: Mug
lesson: A light direction on a simple form.
summary: A light direction on a simple form.
author: claude

tips.title: Look at the mug.
tips.text: The light comes from the left, so the same blue runs light, mid and dark from left to right, in straight bands.

tips.title: Bands follow the form.
tips.text: A round side turns away from the light slowly. Each band is one ramp step, and the handle follows the same rule.

tips.title: Try it.
tips.text: Put the light on the right: with the Pencil, swap the lightest band on the left for the darkest blue. The mug turns round, because the light decides the bands.

title: Potted plant
lesson: Two materials, each with its own ramp.
summary: Two materials, each with its own ramp.
author: claude

tips.title: Look at the two materials.
tips.text: Clay and leaf each have a ramp of their own. The pot runs along Brick and the plant along Greens, and no color is shared, so they stay apart.

tips.title: One flat color each.
tips.text: Before any shading, each material gets the middle step of its ramp. Decide what is made of what here.

tips.title: Try it.
tips.text: Pick Lighten / Darken and stroke across the pot, then across a leaf. Each stays on its own ramp, so clay stays clay and leaf stays leaf.

title: Umbrella
lesson: Curves by pixel runs: 1, 2, 3, not jaggies.
summary: Curves by pixel runs: 1, 2, 3, not jaggies.
author: claude

tips.title: Look at the curve.
tips.text: Follow the top edge from the tip down one side. The edge is drawn in runs of pixels, and it looks smooth because their lengths change in order.

tips.title: Count the runs.
tips.text: From the top: 8, 3, 2, then 1 again and again. Then the edge turns and the runs go down, 1, 2 and longer. A run that breaks that order is a jaggy.

tips.title: Try it.
tips.text: With the Pencil, add one pixel on top of the curve. One run out of order shows as a bump at once. Undo it and the curve is smooth again.
